issues.title: Some buttons do not say what they do
issues.who: Screen reader users hear just "button" and have to guess what pressing it will do. Voice control users cannot name it to press it.
issues.why: The button has no text inside it, usually because it only shows an icon, like a magnifying glass, a heart or a close cross.
issues.fix: Put a short word inside the button. If the design only shows an icon, add an aria-label that says what the button does, and hide the icon from screen readers.

issues.title: Some text is hard to read
issues.who: People with low vision, older visitors, and anyone reading on a phone in sunlight.
issues.why: The text colour is too close to the background colour.
issues.fix: Make the text darker or the background lighter. Normal text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1. Large text needs 3 to 1.

issues.title: The page has no name
issues.who: Screen reader users hear the page name first when it opens, so without one they cannot tell where they landed. Anyone with lots of tabs open sees a blank tab, or just the web address, and has to click through to find your shop again.
issues.why: The page is missing its title, the short name that shows on the browser tab, in bookmarks and in search results.
issues.fix: Add a title inside the head of the page that names the page first and the shop second. Most shop builders have a "page title" or "SEO title" box for this.

issues.title: Headings skip a level
issues.who: Screen reader users often jump from heading to heading to get a quick outline of the page. When a level is skipped, it sounds like a section is missing, and they cannot tell which parts belong together.
issues.why: A heading jumps more than one level down from the one before it, for example from the main page heading straight to a third-level heading. This often happens when a heading size is picked for how it looks rather than where it sits on the page.
issues.fix: Go down one level at a time: the page heading first, then second-level headings for each section, then third-level ones inside those. If you want a heading to look smaller, change its size in the theme settings instead of picking a lower level.

issues.title: The page does not say which language it is in
issues.who: Screen readers pick the wrong voice and pronounce every word badly.
issues.why: The <html> tag has no lang attribute.
issues.fix: Add the language code to the <html> tag, for example lang="de" for German or lang="en" for English.

issues.title: Images have no description
issues.who: Blind visitors using a screen reader. It reads the file name or skips the image.
issues.why: The image has no alt text.
issues.fix: Add an alt attribute that says what the image shows. For pure decoration, use an empty alt="" so screen readers skip it.

issues.title: Form fields have no label
issues.who: Screen reader users hear "edit text" with no idea what to type. Voice control users cannot name the field.
issues.why: The input has no label connected to it, so it has no name.
issues.fix: Add a <label> with a for attribute that matches the input id. Placeholder text is not a good replacement because it disappears as soon as someone types.

issues.title: Some links do not say where they go
issues.who: Screen reader users hear just "link" with no idea where it leads. Voice control users have no word to say to click it.
issues.why: The link has no text inside it, often because it only holds an icon, like a cart or a social media logo.
issues.fix: Put a few words inside the link. If the design only shows an icon, add an aria-label to the link that says where it goes, and hide the icon itself from screen readers.
